t: 1816 was the year without a summer
b: The 1815 eruption of Mount Tambora in Indonesia threw so much ash into the sky that 1816 brought snow in June in parts of North America and failed harvests across Europe. Stuck indoors that gloomy summer, Mary Shelley began writing Frankenstein.

q.p: Which novel was born in the 'year without a summer'?

rq.p: What caused the cold of 1816?

why: Volcanic particles in the stratosphere reflect sunlight.

t: Krakatoa was heard 4,800 km away
b: When Krakatoa erupted in 1883, the explosion was heard on an island near Mauritius, about 4,800 km away. It's often called the loudest sound in recorded history, and pressure waves circled the globe several times.

q.p: How far away was Krakatoa's 1883 eruption heard?

rq.p: What did Krakatoa's pressure waves do?

why: The explosion was one of the most powerful in history.

t: Tutankhamun's tomb was found nearly intact
b: In 1922, Howard Carter found the tomb of the young pharaoh Tutankhamun in Egypt's Valley of the Kings. Most royal tombs had been robbed, but this one still held over 5,000 objects, including the famous gold mask.

q.p: Why was Tutankhamun's tomb such a big find?

rq.p: Who found the tomb in 1922?

why: Its entrance was hidden by debris from a later tomb.

t: The Library of Alexandria faded slowly
b: The popular story has the great library destroyed in one dramatic fire. Historians think it declined over centuries through funding cuts, political purges, war damage and neglect. Julius Caesar's fire in 48 BC did harm, but the library survived it.

q.p: How did the Library of Alexandria end, most historians think?

rq.p: Did the library survive Julius Caesar's fire?

why: Losing support and scholars was more damaging than any single fire.

t: Ancient Egyptians revered cats
b: Cats were linked to the goddess Bastet in ancient Egypt, and many were mummified. The Greek historian Diodorus reported a Roman who accidentally killed a cat being lynched by an angry crowd.

q.p: Which goddess were cats linked with in ancient Egypt?

rq.p: What did Egyptians often do with cats after death?

why: Cats protected grain stores from mice and snakes.

t: Pineapples were 18th-century status symbols
b: In 1700s Britain, pineapples had to be grown in heated hothouses or imported, and cost a fortune. They became symbols of wealth: they appear carved on buildings, and some people reportedly rented one just to show off at a party.

q.p: What did pineapples symbolise in 1700s Britain?

rq.p: How were pineapples grown in Britain?

why: Rarity and cost made them luxury displays.

t: The printing press spread the Reformation
b: When Martin Luther published his 95 Theses in 1517, printing presses copied his arguments fast. Within weeks his ideas spread across Germany, and printed pamphlets helped the Protestant Reformation grow faster than earlier church reform movements.

q.p: What technology helped Luther's ideas spread fast?

rq.p: When did Luther publish his 95 Theses?

why: Earlier reformers relied on handwritten copies and preaching.

t: The first photo of a person was an accident
b: In 1838, Louis Daguerre photographed a busy Paris boulevard. The exposure took several minutes, so moving traffic vanished. But a man stood still having his boots shined, making him likely the first person ever photographed.

q.p: Why does Daguerre's busy 1838 street photo look empty?

rq.p: Who was likely the first person photographed?
o: A man getting his boots shined

why: Long exposures only capture things that stay still.

t: The QWERTY layout is from typewriters
b: Christopher Latham Sholes developed the QWERTY layout in the 1870s for early typewriters. One popular explanation is that it separated common letter pairs to reduce jams. Despite better layouts since, QWERTY stuck because everyone had learned it.

q.p: Where does the QWERTY keyboard layout come from?

rq.p: Why has QWERTY lasted?

why: Switching costs keep old standards alive.

t: The longest-reigning monarch ruled 72 years
b: Louis XIV of France became king in 1643 aged four and reigned until 1715, about 72 years. That's the longest recorded reign of any monarch of a sovereign country. Elizabeth II reigned 70 years.

q.p: Who reigned longest of any sovereign monarch?

rq.p: How old was Louis XIV when he became king?

why: Starting very young is the key to a record reign.

t: Ancient Egyptians used a 365-day calendar
b: The ancient Egyptians had a civil calendar of 365 days: twelve months of 30 days plus five extra days. They tied their year to the yearly flood of the Nile. Our calendar descends partly from it, via the Romans.

q.p: How many days were in the ancient Egyptian civil year?

rq.p: What natural event anchored Egypt's year?

why: Farming depended on predicting the flood.

t: Queen Victoria survived several assassination attempts
b: Queen Victoria faced at least seven attempts on her life during her reign. None succeeded, and each one tended to boost her popularity with the public.

q.p: How many assassination attempts did Queen Victoria survive?

rq.p: What effect did the attempts have on her popularity?

why: Public sympathy rallied around the monarch.

t: The Wild West wasn't so deadly
b: Western cattle towns had far fewer killings than films suggest. One historian counted 15 homicides in Dodge City across its busiest decade, 1876 to 1885. The famous Gunfight at the O.K. Corral in Tombstone lasted about 30 seconds.

q.p: How long did the Gunfight at the O.K. Corral last?

rq.p: Were Wild West towns as deadly as films show?

why: Many towns banned carrying guns within town limits.

t: The Great Pyramid was the tallest for 3,800 years
b: Built around 2560 BC, the Great Pyramid of Giza was originally about 146 metres tall. It remained the tallest human-made structure in the world for over 3,800 years, until Lincoln Cathedral's spire overtook it in the early 1300s.

q.p: What overtook the Great Pyramid as the tallest structure?

rq.p: About how tall was the Great Pyramid originally?

why: Its outer casing stones were later removed, lowering it.

t: Lincoln Cathedral's spire collapsed in 1548
b: Lincoln Cathedral's central spire took the title of world's tallest structure from the Great Pyramid in the 1300s, rising about 160 metres. It held that record for over 200 years until the spire blew down in a storm in 1548.

q.p: What ended Lincoln Cathedral's record?

rq.p: Which country is Lincoln Cathedral in?

why: Tall wooden and lead spires were vulnerable to storms.

t: Timbuktu was a great centre of learning
b: In the 1300s to 1500s, Timbuktu in Mali was a wealthy trading city and a major centre of Islamic scholarship. Its families kept hundreds of thousands of manuscripts on astronomy, law, medicine and maths, many still preserved today.

q.p: What was medieval Timbuktu famous for?

rq.p: Which modern country is Timbuktu in?

why: Trans-Saharan trade in gold and salt brought wealth and scholars.

t: Mansa Musa may be history's richest person
b: Mansa Musa ruled the Mali Empire in the 1300s, when it produced much of the world's gold. On his pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324, he gave away so much gold in Cairo that its value fell there for years.

q.p: What happened when Mansa Musa visited Cairo in 1324?

rq.p: Which empire did Mansa Musa rule?

why: Flooding a market with gold lowers its price.

t: The Hundred Years' War lasted 116 years
b: The Hundred Years' War between England and France ran from 1337 to 1453, about 116 years. It wasn't continuous fighting but a series of wars and truces over claims to the French throne.

q.p: How long did the Hundred Years' War actually last?

rq.p: Which two countries fought it?

why: Historians named it later, rounding the length.

t: Lego bricks from 1958 still fit today
b: Lego patented its stud-and-tube brick design in 1958. Bricks made then still click together with ones made today, because the company has kept the dimensions precise to tiny fractions of a millimetre.

q.p: Will a 1958 Lego brick fit a new one?

rq.p: When was the modern Lego brick patented?

why: Tight manufacturing tolerances keep 'clutch power' the same.

t: Ancient Romans had a fire brigade
b: In AD 6, Emperor Augustus created the Vigiles, a force of freedmen that grew to around 7,000, who fought fires and patrolled Rome's streets at night. They used buckets, pumps, axes and blankets soaked in vinegar.

q.p: Who were Rome's Vigiles?

rq.p: Which emperor set up the Vigiles?

why: Crowded wooden housing made fire a constant danger.

t: Ketchup was once sold as medicine
b: In the 1830s, an American doctor named John Cook Bennett promoted tomato ketchup as a cure for indigestion and other ailments. Tomato 'pills' became a fad before the claims were exposed as nonsense.

q.p: How was tomato ketchup promoted in the 1830s?

rq.p: What happened to the tomato pill craze?

why: Patent medicines were largely unregulated then.

t: Abraham Lincoln is in the wrestling hall of fame
b: As a young man, Abraham Lincoln was a skilled wrestler, reportedly losing only one of around 300 matches. In 1992 he was honoured by the US National Wrestling Hall of Fame.

q.p: What sport was Abraham Lincoln known for as a young man?

rq.p: How many matches did Lincoln reportedly lose?

why: Frontier wrestling was a popular contest of strength.

t: The Colosseum could be flooded, perhaps
b: Ancient writers describe mock sea battles staged in Rome's Colosseum. Historians think early in its life the arena may have been flooded for shows, before the underground rooms and lifts were built under the floor.

q.p: What might the Colosseum have been flooded for?

rq.p: What later made flooding impossible?
o: Underground rooms built below the arena

why: The hypogeum's tunnels and lifts filled the space below the floor.

t: The first speeding ticket was for 8 mph
b: In 1896, Walter Arnold of Kent was fined for driving at about 8 mph in a 2 mph zone, often cited as the world's first speeding conviction. British law then also required a person to walk ahead of some vehicles.

q.p: How fast was the first speeding driver going?

rq.p: What was the speed limit he broke?

why: Early motoring laws treated cars like slow steam engines.

t: Alexander the Great never lost a battle
b: Alexander the Great became king of Macedon at 20 and by 32 had built an empire from Greece to India. Ancient historians record no defeat in a major battle. He died in Babylon in 323 BC, aged 32.

q.p: How old was Alexander the Great when he died?

rq.p: Where did Alexander die?

why: His speed and tactics overwhelmed much larger armies.
